dmm-2008-power-01a.title: Isosceles triangles
dmm-2008-power-01a.body:
Draw $OB$. Triangles $OAB$ and $OBC$ are isosceles ($OA=OB=OC$). Put $\alpha=\angle OBA=\angle OAB$ and $\beta=\angle OBC=\angle OCB$, so $\angle AOB=180^\circ-2\alpha$ and $\angle BOC=180^\circ-2\beta$.

*Case 1: $O$ lies inside triangle $ABC$* (or on side $AC$). Then $\angle ABC=\alpha+\beta$ and the three angles at $O$ add up to $360^\circ$ (to $180^\circ$ on the line $AC$): $\angle AOC=360^\circ-\angle AOB-\angle BOC=2\alpha+2\beta=2\angle ABC$. If $O\in AC$ then $\alpha+\beta=\angle ABC$ and $\angle AOB+\angle BOC=180^\circ$, so $\angle AOC=180^\circ=2(\alpha+\beta)$ as $\alpha+\beta=90^\circ$.

*Case 2: $O$ is on the same side of $AC$ as $B$ but outside the triangle*, say beyond side $AB$ (the case beyond $BC$ is symmetric). Then ray $BA$ lies inside $\angle OBC$, so $\angle ABC=\beta-\alpha$, and ray $OC$ lies inside $\angle AOB$, so $\angle AOC=\angle AOB-\angle COB=(180^\circ-2\alpha)-(180^\circ-2\beta)=2(\beta-\alpha)=2\angle ABC$. ∎

dmm-2008-power-01b.title: Same idea, other configuration
dmm-2008-power-01b.body:
Draw $OB$ and let $\alpha=\angle OBA$, $\beta=\angle OBC$; as before $\angle AOB=180^\circ-2\alpha$, $\angle BOC=180^\circ-2\beta$ by the isosceles triangles $OAB$, $OBC$.

Since $B$ and $O$ lie on opposite sides of $AC$, segment $BO$ meets line $AC$ (at a point of the chord $AC$, which lies inside the circle), so the ray $BO$ lies inside $\angle ABC$ and $\angle ABC=\alpha+\beta$. For the same reason ray $OB$ lies inside $\angle AOC$, so $\angle AOC=\angle AOB+\angle BOC=360^\circ-2(\alpha+\beta)=360^\circ-2\angle ABC$.

If $O$ lies on $AC$ the same computation gives $\angle AOC=180^\circ=360^\circ-2\cdot90^\circ$. If $B$ is on line $AC$ the statement is degenerate. ∎

dmm-2008-power-01c.title: Equal angles
dmm-2008-power-01c.body:
Let $O$ be the center. $A$ and $B$ lie on the same side of line $CD$ (they are on the same arc cut off by chord $CD$). If $O$ is on that side too, then 1A gives $\angle COD=2\angle CAD=2\angle CBD$. If $O$ is on the other side or on $CD$, 1B gives $\angle COD=360^\circ-2\angle CAD=360^\circ-2\angle CBD$ (and $\angle CAD=\angle CBD=90^\circ$ if $O\in CD$). Either way $\angle CAD=\angle CBD$.

*Supplementary angles.* $B$ and $D$ lie on opposite sides of line $AC$. If $O$ is on $B$'s side of $AC$, then 1A for $B$ gives $\angle AOC=2\angle ABC$ and 1B for $D$ gives $\angle AOC=360^\circ-2\angle ADC$; equating, $\angle ABC+\angle ADC=180^\circ$. If $O$ is on $D$'s side the roles swap, and if $O\in AC$ both angles are $90^\circ$. ∎

dmm-2008-power-01d.title: Argue by contradiction
dmm-2008-power-01d.body:
Let $\omega$ be the circle through $B,C,D$ and suppose $A\notin\omega$. Line $AD$ meets $\omega$ again at $E\ne D$ (if the line is tangent at $D$ see below). $A$ and $B$ are on the same side of $CD$, and $\angle CAD=\angle CBD$.

*$E$ on ray $DA$.* Then $E$ is on the same side of $CD$ as $B$, so by 1C (equal angles on chord $CD$) $\angle CED=\angle CBD=\angle CAD$. But $E\ne A$ are two points on ray $DA$: if $A$ is between $D$ and $E$, then $\angle CAD$ is an exterior angle of triangle $CAE$ so $\angle CAD>\angle CEA=\angle CED$; if $E$ is between $D$ and $A$, then $\angle CED$ is exterior in triangle $CEA$ so $\angle CED>\angle CAE=\angle CAD$. Both contradict $\angle CED=\angle CAD$.

*$E$ on the opposite ray (so $D$ is between $A$ and $E$).* Then $E$ and $B$ are on opposite sides of $CD$, and 1C gives $\angle CED+\angle CBD=180^\circ$, so $\angle CED+\angle CAD=180^\circ$. But in triangle $ACE$ the angles at $A$ and $E$ are $\angle CAD$ and $\angle CED$ and they add up to less than $180^\circ$. Contradiction.

*Tangent case.* If $AD$ is tangent to $\omega$ at $D$, the tangent–chord theorem gives $\angle CDA=180^\circ-\angle CBD$ (as $B$ and $A$ are on the same side of $CD$), so in triangle $ACD$ the angles at $A$ and $D$ sum to $180^\circ$, impossible.

Hence $A\in\omega$, i.e. $ABCD$ is cyclic. ∎

dmm-2008-power-01e.title: Argue by contradiction
dmm-2008-power-01e.body:
Let $\omega$ be the circle through $A,B,C$ and suppose $D\notin\omega$. Line $CD$ meets $\omega$ again at $E\ne C$ (tangent case below). Since $\angle ABC+\angle ADC=180^\circ$ we have $\angle ADC=180^\circ-\angle ABC$.

*$E$ on ray $CD$* (so $E$ is on the same side of $AC$ as $D$, opposite to $B$). Then $ABCE$ is cyclic with $B,E$ on opposite sides of $AC$, so $\angle AEC=180^\circ-\angle ABC=\angle ADC$. Now $D\ne E$ are on one ray from $C$: if $E$ is between $C$ and $D$, then $\angle AEC$ is an exterior angle of triangle $AED$, so $\angle AEC>\angle ADE=\angle ADC$; if $D$ is between $C$ and $E$, then $\angle ADC$ is exterior in triangle $ADE$ and $\angle ADC>\angle AED=\angle AEC$. Both contradict $\angle AEC=\angle ADC$.

*$E$ on the opposite ray from $C$ (so $C$ lies between $D$ and $E$).* Then $E$ is on $B$'s side of $AC$, so $\angle AEC=\angle ABC$ (equal angles, 1C), hence $\angle ADC+\angle AEC=180^\circ$. But in triangle $ADE$ these are two of its angles, so their sum is less than $180^\circ$. Contradiction.

*Tangent case.* If $CD$ is tangent to $\omega$ at $C$, the tangent–chord theorem gives an angle equal to an inscribed angle and leads to the same contradiction as above.

Therefore $D\in\omega$. ∎

dmm-2008-power-02a1.title: Angle sum in triangle CKD
dmm-2008-power-02a1.body:
$K$ is the incenter of $\triangle ACD$, so $CK$ and $DK$ bisect $\angle ACD$ and $\angle ADC$. In triangle $CKD$:
$$\angle CKD=180^\circ-\tfrac12\angle ACD-\tfrac12\angle ADC=180^\circ-\tfrac12(180^\circ-\angle CAD)=90^\circ+\tfrac12\angle CAD.\ ∎$$

dmm-2008-power-02a2.title: Equal angles on CD
dmm-2008-power-02a2.body: The same computation in triangle $BCD$ (incenter $J$) gives $\angle CJD=90^\circ+\tfrac12\angle CBD$. Since $ABCD$ is cyclic, $\angle CAD=\angle CBD$ (Equal Angles Theorem), so $\angle CKD=90^\circ+\tfrac12\angle CAD=90^\circ+\tfrac12\angle CBD=\angle CJD$. The points $J$ and $K$ lie inside triangles $BCD$ and $ACD$, hence on the same side of line $CD$ as $A$ and $B$. By the Equal Angles Theorem, $CJKD$ is cyclic. ∎

dmm-2008-power-02a4.title: Opposite angles of CJKD
dmm-2008-power-02a4.body:
Order the four points of the circle through $C,J,K,D$. At $C$ the ray $CJ$ makes the angle $\tfrac12\angle BCD$ with $CD$ ($J$ is the incenter of $BCD$), and the ray $CK$ makes the angle $\tfrac12\angle ACD$ with $CD$; because $A$ lies inside $\angle BCD$, $\angle ACD<\angle BCD$. Points of the circle seen from $C$ at a larger angle with $CD$ are closer to $C$ along the arc, so the order along the arc is $C,J,K,D$ and $CJKD$ is a convex quadrilateral in which $K$ and $C$ are opposite vertices.

By the Supplementary Angles Theorem, $\angle JKD+\angle JCD=180^\circ$. Since $CJ$ bisects $\angle BCD$, $\angle JCD=\tfrac12\angle BCD$. Therefore $\angle JKD=180^\circ-\tfrac12\angle BCD$. ∎

dmm-2008-power-02a5.title: Add the two relations
dmm-2008-power-02a5.body:
By the same argument applied to the cyclic quadrilateral $DKLA$ (with $L$ the incenter of $ABD$): $\angle LKD=180^\circ-\tfrac12\angle BAD$. Hence
$$\angle LKD+\angle JKD=360^\circ-\tfrac12(\angle BAD+\angle BCD)=360^\circ-\tfrac12\cdot180^\circ=270^\circ,$$
because $ABCD$ is cyclic, so $\angle BAD+\angle BCD=180^\circ$ (Supplementary Angles Theorem). Consequently $\angle JKL=360^\circ-270^\circ=90^\circ$, and repeating the argument at the other vertices shows that $IJKL$ has four right angles. ∎

dmm-2008-power-02b.title: A bisector direction and a reflection
dmm-2008-power-02b.body:
Name the angles (equal angles on common chords): $\gamma=\angle CBD=\angle CAD$, $\delta=\angle ACB=\angle ADB$, $\beta=\angle ACD=\angle ABD$. Measure directions of lines counter-clockwise from line $BC$, with $A,D$ above $BC$.

*Step 1: line $IJ$ is parallel to a bisector of the directions of $AC$ and $BD$.* Line $AC$ has direction $\delta$ and line $BD$ has direction $-\gamma$. Since $\angle BIC=90^\circ+\tfrac12\angle BAC$ and $\angle BJC=90^\circ+\tfrac12\angle BDC$ (as in (i)) and $\angle BAC=\angle BDC$, the points $B,C,J,I$ are concyclic. By the inscribed angle theorem (directed angles mod $180^\circ$), $\measuredangle(IJ,IB)=\measuredangle(CJ,CB)$, so
$$\measuredangle(IJ,BC)=\measuredangle(CJ,CB)+\measuredangle(BI,BC).$$
Ray $CJ$ makes the angle $\tfrac12(\delta+\beta)$ with $CB$ ($CJ$ bisects $\angle BCD=\delta+\beta$) and line $BI$ makes the angle $\tfrac12(\beta+\gamma)$ with $BC$ ($BI$ bisects $\angle ABC=\beta+\gamma$), in the opposite rotational senses, so $\measuredangle(IJ,BC)=-\tfrac12(\delta+\beta)+\tfrac12(\beta+\gamma)=\tfrac12(\gamma-\delta)$. Thus line $IJ$ has direction $\tfrac12(\delta-\gamma)$, exactly the average of $\delta$ and $-\gamma$: it is parallel to a bisector of the angle between lines $AC$ and $BD$.

*Step 2: reflection.* The side $JK$ of the rectangle is perpendicular to $IJ$. Let $M$ be the center of the rectangle and let $\sigma$ be the reflection in the line through $M$ parallel to $IJ$. It maps the rectangle to itself, swapping $I\leftrightarrow L$ and $J\leftrightarrow K$. Because its axis has the bisecting direction, $\sigma$ interchanges the directions of $AC$ and $BD$. Therefore $\sigma(\ell_1)$ is the line through $L$ parallel to $BD$, i.e. $\ell_4$, and $\sigma(\ell_3)=\ell_2$.

An isometry preserves distances between lines, so $\operatorname{dist}(\ell_1,\ell_3)=\operatorname{dist}(\ell_4,\ell_2)=:w$. The two pairs of parallel lines form a parallelogram whose side lengths are $w/\sin\varphi$ for both pairs ($\varphi$ is the angle between $AC$ and $BD$), so all four sides are equal: it is a rhombus. ∎

dmm-2008-power-02c.title: Widths of the rhombus are inradius sums
dmm-2008-power-02c.body:
A quadrilateral has exactly two triangulations: by diagonal $AC$ (triangles $ABC,ACD$) or by diagonal $BD$ (triangles $BCD,ABD$).

$I$ is the incenter of $ABC$, so it lies on the same side of $AC$ as $B$ at distance $r_{ABC}$ from $AC$; $K$ lies on the other side of $AC$ (the side of $D$) at distance $r_{ACD}$. The lines $\ell_1,\ell_3$ are parallel to $AC$ through $I,K$, so the distance between them is $r_{ABC}+r_{ACD}$. In the same way $\operatorname{dist}(\ell_2,\ell_4)=r_{BCD}+r_{ABD}$.

In a rhombus the distances between the two pairs of opposite sides are equal (both equal area/side). Hence $r_{ABC}+r_{ACD}=r_{BCD}+r_{ABD}$, which says that the two triangulations have the same sum of inradii. ∎

dmm-2008-power-02d.title: Fan triangulation and one flip
dmm-2008-power-02d.body:
Let $\mathcal P=P_1P_2\cdots P_{n+1}$ be cyclic and let $T_0$ be the *fan* from $P_1$ (diagonals $P_1P_3,\dots,P_1P_n$). Let $T$ be any triangulation; we show $\Sigma_T=\Sigma_{T_0}$ (sum of inradii).

*Case 1: $T$ contains a diagonal $P_1P_j$.* This diagonal also belongs to $T_0$ and cuts $\mathcal P$ into two cyclic polygons with at most $n$ sides. $T$ and $T_0$ induce triangulations of each of them, and by the induction hypothesis these have equal sums of inradii. Adding the two parts, $\Sigma_T=\Sigma_{T_0}$.

*Case 2: $T$ contains no diagonal from $P_1$.* Then the only triangle at $P_1$ is $P_{n+1}P_1P_2$, so $P_2P_{n+1}\in T$. The triangle of $T$ on the other side of $P_2P_{n+1}$ is $P_2P_mP_{n+1}$ for some $3\le m\le n$. The cyclic quadrilateral $P_1P_2P_mP_{n+1}$ is triangulated in $T$ by the diagonal $P_2P_{n+1}$. Replace this diagonal by $P_1P_m$: by the four-sided case (previous problem) the sum of the two inradii does not change. The new triangulation $T'$ contains $P_1P_m$, so Case 1 gives $\Sigma_{T'}=\Sigma_{T_0}$, hence $\Sigma_T=\Sigma_{T'}=\Sigma_{T_0}$.

So all triangulations of a cyclic $(n+1)$-gon have the same sum of inradii, completing the induction (the base cases being triangles and quadrilaterals). ∎

dmm-2008-power-03a.title: Trigonometric proof
dmm-2008-power-03a.body:
When $O$ is outside or on the boundary, one angle of the triangle is obtuse or right (this is exactly when one of the distances is negative or zero), so this is the case where the signs in the definition matter. The following computation works for all triangles, in particular this case.

Since $D,E,F$ are the midpoints of $AB,AC,BC$, in the isosceles triangle $OAB$ the segment $OD$ bisects the central angle. If $\angle C$ is acute, then $C$ and $O$ are on the same side of $AB$ and $\angle AOB=2\angle C$ (1A), so $OD=R\cos C>0$ and the segment $OD$ enters the triangle: $\|OD\|=R\cos C$. If $\angle C$ is obtuse, $O$ and $C$ are on opposite sides of $AB$, $\angle AOB=360^\circ-2C$ (1B), $OD=R\cos(180^\circ-C)=-R\cos C$ and the segment $OD$ lies outside the triangle, so again $\|OD\|=R\cos C$ (negative). If $C=90^\circ$, $O=D$ and both sides are $0$. Likewise $\|OE\|=R\cos B$ and $\|OF\|=R\cos A$. Hence
$$\|OD\|+\|OE\|+\|OF\|=R(\cos A+\cos B+\cos C).$$
Now $\cos A+\cos B=2\sin\tfrac C2\cos\tfrac{A-B}2$ and $\cos C=1-2\sin^2\tfrac C2$ with $\sin\tfrac C2=\cos\tfrac{A+B}2$, so
$$\cos A+\cos B+\cos C=1+2\sin\tfrac C2\left(\cos\tfrac{A-B}2-\cos\tfrac{A+B}2\right)=1+4\sin\tfrac A2\sin\tfrac B2\sin\tfrac C2.$$
Finally $r=4R\sin\frac A2\sin\frac B2\sin\frac C2$: in triangle $AIB$, $\angle AIB=90^\circ+\tfrac C2$, so by the law of sines $AI=\dfrac{AB\sin(B/2)}{\cos(C/2)}=\dfrac{2R\sin C\sin(B/2)}{\cos(C/2)}=4R\sin\tfrac C2\sin\tfrac B2$, and $r=AI\sin\tfrac A2$. Therefore the sum equals $R+r$. ∎

dmm-2008-power-03b.title: Acute triangle
dmm-2008-power-03b.body:
Here $\angle A,\angle B,\angle C\le90^\circ$, so all three signs are $+$ and

Since $D,E,F$ are the midpoints of $AB,AC,BC$, in the isosceles triangle $OAB$ the segment $OD$ bisects the central angle. If $\angle C$ is acute, then $C$ and $O$ are on the same side of $AB$ and $\angle AOB=2\angle C$ (1A), so $OD=R\cos C>0$ and the segment $OD$ enters the triangle: $\|OD\|=R\cos C$. If $\angle C$ is obtuse, $O$ and $C$ are on opposite sides of $AB$, $\angle AOB=360^\circ-2C$ (1B), $OD=R\cos(180^\circ-C)=-R\cos C$ and the segment $OD$ lies outside the triangle, so again $\|OD\|=R\cos C$ (negative). If $C=90^\circ$, $O=D$ and both sides are $0$. Likewise $\|OE\|=R\cos B$ and $\|OF\|=R\cos A$. Hence
$$\|OD\|+\|OE\|+\|OF\|=R(\cos A+\cos B+\cos C).$$
Now $\cos A+\cos B=2\sin\tfrac C2\cos\tfrac{A-B}2$ and $\cos C=1-2\sin^2\tfrac C2$ with $\sin\tfrac C2=\cos\tfrac{A+B}2$, so
$$\cos A+\cos B+\cos C=1+2\sin\tfrac C2\left(\cos\tfrac{A-B}2-\cos\tfrac{A+B}2\right)=1+4\sin\tfrac A2\sin\tfrac B2\sin\tfrac C2.$$
Finally $r=4R\sin\frac A2\sin\frac B2\sin\frac C2$: in triangle $AIB$, $\angle AIB=90^\circ+\tfrac C2$, so by the law of sines $AI=\dfrac{AB\sin(B/2)}{\cos(C/2)}=\dfrac{2R\sin C\sin(B/2)}{\cos(C/2)}=4R\sin\tfrac C2\sin\tfrac B2$, and $r=AI\sin\tfrac A2$. Therefore the sum equals $R+r$. ∎

dmm-2008-power-03c.title: Add Carnot's formula over all triangles
dmm-2008-power-03c.body:
A triangulation of the $n$-gon has $n-2$ triangles, all inscribed in the same circle. By Carnot, for each triangle $T$: $r_T=\sum_{\text{sides }s\text{ of }T}\|O s\|_T-R$, where $\|Os\|_T$ is the signed distance (positive iff $O$ is on the same side of the line $s$ as $T$; this agrees with the definition because the interior of $OQ$ near the foot $Q$ lies in $T$ exactly when $O$ is on $T$'s side). Summing over the $n-2$ triangles,
$$\sum r_T=\sum_T\sum_{s\subset T}\|Os\|_T-R(n-2).$$
Each *diagonal* is a side of exactly two triangles, lying on opposite sides of it. The signed distance changes sign between the two sides (if $O$ is on the line both are $0$), so the two contributions cancel. Each *side of $\mathcal P$* belongs to exactly one triangle, whose side of the line is the side of $\mathcal P$, so it contributes $\|OQ_i\|$ with the sign prescribed in the problem. Therefore
$$\sum r_T=\|OQ_1\|+\cdots+\|OQ_n\|-R(n-2).\ ∎$$

dmm-2008-power-03d.title: Independence
dmm-2008-power-03d.body: The right-hand side $\|OQ_1\|+\cdots+\|OQ_n\|-R(n-2)$ is determined by the polygon alone (its circumcenter $O$, circumradius $R$, number of sides $n$ and the signed distances $\|OQ_i\|$ to its sides). It does not mention the triangulation. Since it equals the sum of the inradii for every triangulation, all triangulations give the same sum. ∎
